status: candidate / pending_human_review (model reading, round 21 second round; not an operator gate)
dataset_family: Xiangya Hospital (Central South University, Changsha) Endocrinology Department, inpatients hospitalised for T2DM, March 2021 to December 2022. Hospital case-control design: 1,001 participants (274 MCI / 727 controls), split 705 training / 296 validation. No other corpus block reports this sample.
method_family: Chi-square screening, multivariable logistic regression and a CHAID decision tree on binary demographic, lifestyle and record-extracted T2DM variables. Diabetic retinopathy is a yes/no complication 'extracted from medical records'. No ocular examination is described, and no ocular measure is acquired or analysed.
what_it_shows:
Maimaitituerxun R, Chen W, Xiang J, Xie Y, Xiao F, Wu XY, Chen L, Yang J, Liu A, Dai W (2024), Brain and Behavior 14:e3456.
- In the training set, record-coded DR was more frequent in MCI cases (49.2% vs 34.4%).
- DR remained one of six variables independently associated with MCI: aOR 1.55 (1.02-2.35), p = .042.
- DR was one of six CHAID tree predictors. The whole-model AUC in validation was 0.67 for the tree and 0.69 for logistic regression.
- The paper never reports DR-specific discrimination.
why:
IDENTITY. The PDF's title, authors (Rehanguli Maimaitituerxun ... Wenjie Dai; Xiangya School of Public Health) and DOI 10.1002/brb3.3456 match the block, whose header is the file name. I read the whole extract, pp.1-9, up to the reference list.

STATED FORM, no. The statement concerns ocular channels, retinal structure or eye-movement behaviour, as biomarker directions. This study acquires and analyses no ocular measurement. DR is a binary comorbidity field: 'T2DM-related information was extracted from medical records' (p.3). The paper never says how, when or by whom DR was diagnosed; no funduscopy, photography, grading scheme or ophthalmologist is mentioned. DR enters as one of 19 candidate predictors of a risk model. Its adjusted association is borderline (lower CI bound 1.02, p = .042) among 17 covariates, with no multiplicity correction, and no DR-only discrimination is reported. The authors frame DR and nephropathy as microvascular complications to be managed (p.8), not as a detection biomarker for cognitive decline.

This matches the round-1 verdict on P-1152, where a DR comorbidity field in a routine-variable model was scored no. It differs from P-688 in two ways: P-688 performed funduscopy by a retinal specialist to ETDRS criteria for the study, and it reports a DR-specific AUC. This is the boundary case. If the operator counts a record-coded DR diagnosis as retinal-structure evidence, the stated verdict would be partly at most, in a different population (hospitalised T2DM), and never yes, because nothing about scalable detection is shown.

NARROWED FORM, no. No ocular measure is taken, so the study cannot show an ocular measure's association with MCI in the sense the wording uses (retinal imaging, saccadic measures).

SOURCE QUALITY. These are reporting errors I noticed; they do not affect the DR row, whose counts are internally consistent (94/191 = 49.2%, 177/514 = 34.4%, total 271 + 117 = 388).
- Table 1 prints DR 'No 613 (6.2)', a typo for 61.2%.
- Table 1 smoking and drinking totals do not equal the training plus validation columns: 561 non-smokers in total against 565 + 235 = 800.
- In Table 2 the primary-caregiver case counts (104 + 170 = 274) are the full-sample case total rather than the 191 training cases, and the nephropathy percentages (31.4%, 50.0%) do not match their counts.
MCI is defined by physician-applied Petersen criteria with MMSE cut-offs (p.3). The authors concede a hospital-based design and no external validation (p.8).

INDEPENDENCE. A single Changsha hospital. No shared sample, site or authors with P-5, P-952, P-966 or P-105, with the round-1 candidates, or with P-688 (Fuzhou). Not a preprint: a peer-reviewed Wiley article.

DEFECTS NOTED. The registry Modality 'Clinical/tabular' is correct. The block correctly says 'Hospital-based case-control', but the registry study_design_type is 'cross_sectional'.

quotes.quote: This hospital-based case–control study was performed in the Endocrinology Department of Xiangya Hospital affiliated to Central South University between March 2021 and December 2022. MCI was defined based on the Petersen criteria. Demographic characteristics, lifestyle factors, and T2DM-related information were collected.

Demographic characteristics and lifestyle factors were obtained retrospectively through face-to-face interviews by well-qualified investigators. T2DM-related information was extracted from medical records.
diabetic complications (diabetic nephropathy [Yes vs. No], diabetic retinopathy [Yes vs. No], and diabetic foot [Yes vs. No]).

diabetic nephropathy (aOR = 1.68, 95% CI: 1.11–2.56, p = .015), and diabetic retinopathy (aOR = 1.55, 95% CI: 1.02–2.35, p = .042) were predictor variables independently associated with MCI by the multivariate logistic regression analysis.

The AUC value of the decision tree models was .75 (95% CI: .71–.78) and .67 (95% CI: .61–.74) in the training and validation sets, respectively, and that of the multivariate logistic regression models was 0.76 (95% CI: .72–.80) and 0.69 (95% CI: .62–.75) in the training and validation sets, respectively.

Additionally, the impacts of diabetic retinopathy on cognitive function may be explained by the processes of shared pathways, including neuroinflammation and degeneration, vascular degeneration, and glial activation (Little et al., 2022). Therefore, the findings of this study strongly highlighted the importance of strengthening the management of diabetic complications including diabetic nephropathy and retinopathy for maintaining cognitive function of T2DM patients in clinical practice.

First, this study was hospital-based. Therefore, whether the findings of this study can be generalized into those from community settings remains unclear. Second, though internally well validated, there was still a lack of external validation for the findings of this study.
